attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: The wording is firm: reaching AGI requires solving all three problems. 'Kidding themselves' is rhetorical emphasis. The concession about pictures and conversation is kept as a qualifier. No deadline was given.

contract.note: It is fair to read this as a claim that all three are necessary, with an independently defined AGI and 'solved' meaning reliable competence. The contract rightly says that present-day failures do not prove necessity and that no accepted AGI settles nothing.

evidence.note: A 2026 preprint showing that tested models still struggle with abstraction. It covers only a few models and cannot show necessity or settle the global antecedent.
AGI Society, Sept 2026: the evidence for GPT-6 Astra is not enough to conclude AGI, and there is no accepted AGI test. So no established AGI exists as a counterexample.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm claim that AGI needs abstraction, compositionality and the type-token distinction, with no deadline. The packet has no independently accepted AGI that lacks one of these, so the early-resolution rule is not met. Nothing in it shows necessity either. Current limitations and the disputed AGI claims are context only, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own commentary on a study he cites in his post.

semantics.note: Correctly narrowed to the single cited study. 'Straight out of 1993' supports the historical comparison.

contract.note: Reading 'the same stumbling block' as a shared limitation in compositional generalization is the ordinary reading. The contract requires the cited study to be identified, which is reasonable.

reviews.rationale: The abstract Marcus refers to is missing from the post text, and the packet could not identify the study. There is no outcome evidence about its model, measures or results, so the study-specific claim cannot be checked. The statement itself is intact, so this is unresolved rather than an abstention.

attribution.note: Marcus's own summary of Razeghi's study, written in his own post.

semantics.note: The scope is arithmetic in the cited LLM study, which fits the context. 'Only... changed' is rhetorical emphasis on persistence. Not hedged.

contract.note: Reading 'troubles with abstraction' as frequency-dependent, unreliable arithmetic generalization is an ordinary reading, neither stretched for nor against Marcus. 'Last year' = 2022 checks out.

evidence.note: Razeghi et al., May 2022: large frequency-linked performance gaps on arithmetic in GPT-based models. This meets the support condition. The packet oddly lists e1 as counterevidence, but its content supports.

reviews.rationale: The cited 2022 study finds strong frequency-associated gaps on addition and multiplication. That matches the contract's support condition of limited arithmetic generalization tied to familiarity with pretraining data. The study's caveats (correlation, not proof that models lack abstraction) narrow the finding but do not contradict it.
